title: Glia Feed the Axons They Wrap

scenes.tts: Your brain is about two percent of your weight. It uses about twenty percent of the energy you spend at rest. Much of that goes to axons and synapses. A motor axon can run a metre, and myelin wraps most of it. Myelin limits access to the fluid outside. So how is the far end fed?
scenes.visual: Two bars (2 and 20 percent) give way to a long myelinated axon; fluid arrows are blocked; question marks at the far end.
scenes.narration: Your brain is about two percent of your weight. It uses about twenty percent of the energy you spend at rest. Much of that goes to axons and synapses. A motor axon can run a metre, and myelin wraps most of it. Myelin limits access to the fluid outside. So how is the far end fed?

scenes.tts: Start with the cost. Every action potential lets sodium in and potassium out. The sodium potassium pump puts them back. It spends one A T P to move three sodium out and two potassium in. Energy budgets for rodent grey matter put most signalling energy into this pumping. The pumps never rest. An axon cannot send A T P a metre, so it must make it locally.

scenes.visual: Membrane patch: ions leak through channels, pump returns 3 Na out, 2 K in for one ATP; then a long axon where ATP cannot travel and mitochondria make it locally.

scenes.tts: Glial cells make myelin in segments along the axon. That makes them candidate suppliers. Glucose becomes pyruvate, and pyruvate can become lactate. That reaction runs in both directions. Lactate crosses membranes on transporters called M C T s. A cell that takes up lactate can turn it back into pyruvate and burn it. So lactate is a portable fuel.

scenes.visual: Glial cell lying on an axon; glucose to pyruvate to lactate inside the glia with a two-way arrow; lactate crosses an MCT gate and is burned by axon mitochondria.

scenes.tts: Astrocytes are the other candidate. In cultured mouse astrocytes, glutamate made the cells take up more of a glucose analogue and release lactate. From this came the shuttle idea. An active synapse makes its astrocyte release lactate, and the neuron burns it. Some work in mouse cortex reported a lactate gradient from astrocytes to neurons. But imaging of single neurons saw them raise their own glycolysis, with no sign of lactate import. So treat the shuttle as a hypothesis with partial support.
scenes.visual: Astrocyte beside a synapse sends lactate to the neuron (shuttle idea); two cards, evidence for and evidence against; the arrow turns dashed with a hypothesis label.

scenes.tts: The case is firmer for oligodendrocytes. Delete Cox ten in these cells, and they can no longer respire. They live on glycolysis alone. Even so, in the adult brain, myelin and axons were largely preserved. That fits glia feeding axons, but does not show it. The stronger evidence came from the transporter. Lower M C T one, and motor neurons died. In mice, axons also swelled. In culture, lactate protected stressed neurons.

scenes.visual: Oligodendrocyte over an axon: respiration crossed out yet lactate still flows and the axon stays intact; then the MCT gate is blocked, the axon swells; lactate in culture protects.

scenes.tts: Here is the picture. Oligodendrocytes take up glucose, run glycolysis, and export lactate or pyruvate through M C T one. The axon takes it in and burns it in its mitochondria. In mice, myelinating glia appear to support axon metabolism. The route and the size of the contribution are still unsettled. The astrocyte shuttle is still debated.
